13|14,29|Pathogenesis sequence|Which sequence best describes the establishment and spread of infection in the lecture overview?|Entry, attachment, survival and colonization, tissue damage, exit|Exit, tissue damage, attachment, entry, colonization|Antibody production, budding, sporulation, fermentation, exit|Entry, immediate recovery, exit without any microbial interaction|The overview organizes pathogenesis around entry, adherence, overcoming defenses, producing disease and leaving the host.

16|49|Secretory cells|Why does an antibody-secreting plasma cell require extensive protein-synthesis and secretory machinery?|It produces and releases large quantities of immunoglobulin protein|It synthesizes bacterial peptidoglycan|It must photosynthesize to release antibodies|It has to form a tapeworm scolex|The cell comparison emphasizes the large antibody output of B-lineage secretory cells and the machinery needed to support it.

16|3,4|Adaptive immunity|Why is a secondary adaptive response usually faster than a primary response?|Antigen-specific memory cells are already present|All pathogens lose their antigens after first exposure|Innate barriers disappear after the first exposure|Naive cells can no longer divide|Memory B and T cells generated during earlier exposure respond rapidly when the same antigen is encountered again.

16|5,6,9|Lymphocyte development|Which pairing correctly identifies adult lymphocyte maturation sites?|B cells in bone marrow; T cells in thymus|B cells in thymus; T cells in red-cell cytoplasm|Both mature only in the gallbladder|Both mature only on the skin surface|Both lineages originate from marrow precursors but their major maturation sites differ.

16|5,7,8,30|Humoral immunity|Which cells become antibody-secreting plasma cells?|B cells|Neutrophils|Erythrocytes|Mast cells|Humoral immunity depends on B-cell differentiation and antibody secretion by plasma cells.

16|6,7,16,17|Cell-mediated immunity|Which cell type is central to antigen-specific cell-mediated immunity?|T lymphocyte|Red blood cell|Platelet|Bacterial cell|T cells coordinate immune responses or kill target cells; antibodies are produced by B-lineage cells.

16|10|Antigen structure|What is an epitope?|The specific antigenic site recognized by an immune receptor or antibody|The entire spleen|The constant region of every antibody|A type of blood vessel|An antigen can contain multiple epitopes that are recognized separately.

16|11|Alloantigens|Which is an example of an alloantigen system?|ABO blood-group antigens|Every antigen on every bacterial species|A pH indicator in agar|A microbial siderophore only|Alloantigens vary among members of the same species, as illustrated by blood-group markers.

16|11|Superantigens|Why can superantigens produce an unusually large immune response?|They activate large numbers of T cells and can trigger extensive cytokine release|They contain more red blood cells than plasma|They permanently prevent all inflammation|They are all harmless host enzymes|The lecture links excessive T-cell activation with toxic shock and overwhelming cytokine responses.

16|12,14|Clonal expansion|What happens during clonal expansion?|An activated lymphocyte divides into cells with the same antigen specificity|Every lymphocyte loses its receptor|A pathogen makes antibodies against itself|Red blood cells form new nuclei|Expansion increases the number of effector and memory cells specific for the recognized antigen.

16|13,14|Self-tolerance|How does clonal deletion contribute to self-tolerance?|It removes strongly self-reactive developing lymphocytes|It destroys every foreign antigen before birth|It makes every lymphocyte recognize the same microbe|It converts B cells into red blood cells|Removing self-reactive clones reduces the risk of an immune attack on the body's own tissues.

16|17,22|Antigen presentation|Which group contains professional antigen-presenting cells discussed in the lecture?|Dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells|Only erythrocytes and platelets|Only neurons and muscle cells|Only bacteria and viruses|These cells can process antigen and display fragments for recognition by T cells.

16|18|T-cell recognition|What does a conventional T-cell receptor recognize on a presenting cell?|An antigen fragment in association with MHC|Only free lactose|Only an intact antibody Fc region|A bacterial colony's color|T-cell recognition is directed at the peptide-MHC combination rather than isolated soluble antigen alone.

16|19,20,21|CD markers|What does CD4 or CD8 identify in this context?|A cell-surface differentiation marker associated with T-cell subsets|A carbohydrate-fermentation product|A type of bacterial endospore|A vaccine storage temperature|CD molecules help identify and functionally characterize immune-cell populations.

16|23,24,25|MHC restriction|Which pairing is correct for conventional antigen presentation?|MHC II to CD4 T cells; MHC I to CD8 T cells|MHC I only to B-cell antibodies; MHC II only to red cells|MHC II to CD8 exclusively; MHC I to CD4 exclusively|Neither subset recognizes MHC|CD4 and CD8 co-receptors are associated with recognition of different MHC classes.

16|25,26|Helper T cells|Which helper T-cell function is emphasized for Th1 cells?|Activation of macrophages|Secretion of bacterial exotoxin|Formation of erythrocyte membranes|Direct synthesis of every immunoglobulin|The lecture contrasts inflammatory Th1 activity with Th2 help for humoral responses.

16|25,26|Helper T cells|Which helper T-cell function is emphasized for Th2 cells?|Helping activate B-cell responses|Becoming a red blood cell|Producing bacterial LPS|Replacing complement with hemoglobin|Th2-associated signals support B-cell-mediated humoral immunity.

16|27,28|Cytotoxic T cells|Which is an appropriate target for a CD8 cytotoxic T cell?|A virus-infected host cell presenting the relevant antigen|Only an extracellular antibody molecule|Only a bacterial sugar in broth|Only a free red blood cell lacking all presentation|Cytotoxic T cells recognize relevant peptide-MHC I complexes and kill affected host cells.

16|27,28|Cytotoxic mechanisms|How do perforin and granzymes contribute to cytotoxic killing?|They help deliver signals that cause target-cell death|They make new bacterial capsules|They convert antibodies into antigens|They produce a new bone-marrow stem cell|Cytotoxic granule components support destruction of infected or abnormal target cells.

16|31,32|B-cell activation|What can follow binding of antigen to a B cell's membrane immunoglobulin?|Antigen uptake, presentation and differentiation toward an effector response|Immediate conversion into a neutrophil|Loss of all antigen specificity|Formation of a bacterial cell wall|B cells can bind their specific antigen, process it and participate in interactions leading to antibody responses.

16|33,34|Antibodies|Which cells secrete antibodies in the humoral response?|Plasma cells derived from B cells|CD8 T cells|Red blood cells|Neutrophils|Antibodies are products of the B-cell lineage; plasma cells specialize in secretion.

16|34|Antibody measurements|What does an antibody titer help quantify?|The level of antibody reactivity in a sample|The number of bacterial flagella|The temperature of the thymus|The thickness of agar|Titer describes an amount of measurable activity, commonly assessed through serial dilution in an antibody assay.

16|35,36|Antibody structure|What is the usual basic chain composition of an antibody monomer?|Two heavy chains and two light chains|Four identical heavy chains and no light chains|One DNA strand and one RNA strand|Two bacterial walls and one capsule|The Y-shaped immunoglobulin unit contains paired heavy and light polypeptide chains linked by disulfide bonds.

16|35,36|Antibody binding|Which antibody region contains the antigen-binding sites?|Fab arms|Only the Fc stem|Only an unrelated bacterial capsule|Only a host MHC molecule|The Fab portions include variable regions that determine binding specificity.

16|35,40,43|Antibody class|Which region determines an antibody's isotype or class?|The heavy-chain constant region|The pathogen's cell wall|Only the light-chain variable region|The pH of the blood sample|Isotypes such as IgG, IgA and IgM differ in their heavy-chain constant regions and associated functions.

16|37|Antibody diversity|Which mechanisms help generate diverse antibody-binding sites?|Gene-segment rearrangement and mutation of variable-region sequences|Only random mixing of whole red blood cells|Conversion of complement into IgG|Repeated bacterial Gram staining|Rearrangement creates receptor diversity and variable-region mutation can further modify antibody binding.

16|38|Antigen binding|What holds an antibody to its matching antigen at the binding site?|Noncovalent interactions such as hydrogen bonds and electrostatic attraction|A permanent peptidoglycan bond|A new bacterial chromosome|An iron-based metal weld|Antigen-antibody binding involves complementary molecular surfaces held together by multiple noncovalent forces.

16|39|Antibody functions|How does neutralization by antibodies protect the host?|It blocks a toxin or pathogen from interacting with its target|It always directly digests every pathogen|It turns every antigen into glucose|It prevents any phagocyte from reaching microbes|Binding can block attachment or toxin action even before the target is removed by other defenses.

16|39,41|Antibody functions|How can IgG coating enhance removal of a microbe?|Phagocyte Fc receptors can bind the coated target|IgG becomes a red blood cell|IgG prevents every complement reaction|It removes all cell-surface receptors from the host|Antibody-mediated opsonization facilitates uptake through Fc-receptor recognition.

16|41|IgG|Which antibody class is transferred across the placenta to the fetus?|IgG|IgM pentamer|IgE|IgD|Placental IgG transfer supplies passive antibody protection before the infant's own responses mature.

16|41|IgA|Which antibody is especially important in mucosal secretions such as tears, saliva and milk?|IgA|IgD only|IgE only|IgM only in its naive-cell receptor form|Secretory IgA is a prominent mucosal antibody and commonly occurs as a linked dimer.
16|42,44|IgM|Which class is typically secreted first in a primary antibody response?|IgM|IgE|IgD|IgA exclusively|Naive B-cell responses commonly begin with IgM before switching to other classes.

16|42|IgE|Which antibody class binds mast cells and is strongly associated with immediate allergy?|IgE|IgG|IgA|IgD|IgE bound to mast cells or basophils can participate in allergen-triggered mediator release.

16|42|IgD|Where is IgD mainly found according to the lecture?|On B-cell surfaces|Only inside erythrocytes|As a bacterial outer membrane|Only inside fungal spores|IgD is primarily a membrane-associated immunoglobulin of B cells.

16|44,45|Secondary response|What is characteristic of a secondary antibody response to the same antigen?|A faster, stronger response with prominent IgG production|No involvement of memory cells|Only IgD and no other classes|An obligatory loss of specificity|Memory populations enable faster responses and greater amounts of class-switched antibody.

16|44|Class switching|What can remain the same when a B-cell lineage switches antibody class?|Antigen specificity|The heavy-chain constant region|Every effector function|The antibody's isotype|Class switching alters the constant region while retaining antigen-binding specificity.

16|47,48|NK cells|What does the missing-self concept help explain?|NK-cell killing of cells with reduced or altered MHC I signals|Why antibodies bind only to bacterial sugar|Why neutrophils become plasma cells|Why all healthy cells are killed equally|NK-cell responses balance activating and inhibitory signals and can target abnormal cells with deficient self-MHC signals.

16|47,48|NK cells|How do NK cells differ from conventional antigen-specific cytotoxic T cells?|They can respond without prior sensitization to a particular peptide antigen|They produce all secreted antibodies|They mature into bacteria|They require antibody gene rearrangement for every target|NK cells are innate lymphocytes; conventional CD8 responses rely on antigen-specific recognition and activation.

16|50|Active immunity|Which situation is an example of artificially acquired active immunity?|Vaccination that stimulates the recipient's own immune response|Receiving preformed immune globulin|Maternal IgG crossing the placenta|Receiving antibodies in breast milk|Vaccines stimulate the host's own antigen-specific response and can establish memory.

16|50|Passive immunity|Why is passive antibody protection generally temporary?|The recipient receives antibodies without generating the same immune memory from that transfer|The transferred antibodies reproduce indefinitely|It permanently removes all antigens|It replaces the recipient's bone marrow|Transferred antibodies eventually decline; passive transfer does not itself create the recipient's antigen-specific memory response.

16|50,51|Immune memory|How does vaccination prepare for later exposure?|It primes immune memory through an initial antigen-specific response|It prevents all future exposure to the organism|It directly sterilizes every environmental surface|It permanently replaces innate immunity|Vaccination prepares immune responses so later exposure can be controlled more effectively; protection is not guaranteed sterilization.

16|51|Population immunity|How can widespread effective vaccination help protect some nonimmune people?|It reduces opportunities for transmission in the population|It transfers every vaccinated person's antibodies directly into all neighbors|It removes the need for individual immune responses|It makes all microbes incapable of mutation|Reduced circulation can indirectly lower exposure among people who are not immune.

16|52|Vaccine platforms|What distinguishes a live attenuated vaccine?|It contains a weakened form of the organism capable of limited replication|It contains only preformed donor antibodies|It contains only a pH indicator|It contains an untreated highly virulent organism by definition|Attenuation reduces virulence while retaining an organism that can stimulate an immune response.

16|53|Vaccine platforms|What is a subunit vaccine based on?|Selected antigenic components rather than the whole pathogen|Only the patient's own red blood cells|Only ready-made antibodies|Only disinfectant molecules|Subunit approaches expose the immune system to selected pathogen components or products.

16|54,55,56|Genetic vaccine platforms|How does an mRNA vaccine supply its antigenic stimulus?|Host cells use delivered mRNA to make the encoded antigen|The mRNA becomes a bacterial cell wall|The vaccine contains only donor IgG|The vaccine removes all host ribosomes|The delivered instruction is translated to antigen, which can then stimulate immune recognition.

16|55,56|Genetic vaccine platforms|What distinguishes an adenoviral-vector platform from an mRNA-delivery platform?|It uses a viral vector to deliver genetic instructions|It must contain preformed host antibodies|It cannot express an antigen|It works only by directly digesting bacterial walls|The lecture contrasts viral-vector delivery with delivery of mRNA instructions.

16|57,58|Vaccine misconceptions|Which conclusion is supported by the studies discussed in the vaccine-misconceptions slides?|Vaccination has not been shown to cause autism|All reported adverse events prove vaccine causation|Twelve selected cases establish population-level causation|Vaccination eliminates every possible side effect|The lecture rejects the discredited vaccine-autism claim and emphasizes the importance of valid large-scale evidence.

17|3,4,5|Immune disorders|What distinguishes hypersensitivity from immunodeficiency?|Hypersensitivity is a harmful exaggerated response; immunodeficiency is inadequate defense|Both terms mean complete absence of antigens|Hypersensitivity always means a bacterial infection|Immunodeficiency always means excessive IgE|The course contrasts inappropriate overreaction with insufficient immune function.

17|5,6|Type I hypersensitivity|Which antibody class is central to immediate hypersensitivity?|IgE|IgD|IgM alone|IgA alone|IgE-mediated activation of mast cells and basophils is central to the immediate allergic pathway.

17|6|Atopy|Which example fits the lecture's discussion of atopic disease?|Allergic hay fever|An ABO-incompatible transfusion|An Arthus reaction|A positive tuberculin skin test|Atopic conditions are associated with localized or chronic allergic tendencies, unlike the other hypersensitivity examples.

17|7|Anaphylaxis|Which combination explains why anaphylaxis can be life-threatening?|Airway narrowing together with severe vasodilation and falling blood pressure|Only increased red-cell production|Only delayed thickening of the skin|Only a local change in hair color|Widespread mediator release can compromise breathing and circulation.

17|7|Anaphylaxis mechanisms|Which effects explain epinephrine's role in the lecture's anaphylaxis discussion?|Relaxing airway smooth muscle and constricting blood vessels|Producing IgE and dilating all vessels|Digesting red blood cells|Making bacterial endotoxin harmless by fermentation|These effects counter important airway and circulatory disturbances of anaphylaxis.

17|8|Allergen exposure|Which set lists common portals of allergen entry?|Inhalation, ingestion, injection and skin contact|Only bacterial conjugation and transduction|Only lymph flow and red-cell production|Only antigen presentation inside the thymus|The lecture classifies allergens by the route through which the host encounters them.

17|9,10|Type I mechanism|What happens when allergen cross-links appropriate IgE on sensitized mast cells?|Release of inflammatory mediators such as histamine|Immediate production of new red blood cells|Antibody-independent destruction of all lymphocytes|Formation of nitrate reductase|Cross-linking initiates mast-cell activation and mediator release in a sensitized individual.

17|10|Histamine effects|Which effect is consistent with histamine activity in immediate allergy?|Bronchial smooth-muscle constriction and increased vascular effects|Complete blockade of all inflammation|Production of new MHC alleles|Conversion of IgM into bacterial LPS|Histamine contributes to airway and vascular changes associated with allergic symptoms.

17|11|Allergy testing|What does a wheal-and-flare response assess in the lecture's skin-test example?|A localized response to an allergen|The number of bacteria in a urine sample|The oxygen requirement of an isolate|The patient's bacterial Gram reaction|Local swelling and redness can reflect an immediate hypersensitivity response to the tested allergen.

17|12|Allergy treatment mechanisms|How do antihistamines act in the lecture's explanation?|They block histamine receptor effects|They remove every IgE gene|They convert mast cells into erythrocytes|They directly inhibit all bacterial ribosomes|Blocking histamine's action can reduce some symptoms without removing the underlying antigen specificity.

17|12|Desensitization|What is the general aim of allergen desensitization discussed in this topic?|Modify the immune response through controlled repeated allergen exposure|Give a virulent pathogen to every patient|Permanently eliminate all white blood cells|Make the patient produce only IgM against blood cells|Desensitization aims to change the response to an allergen rather than simply blocking symptoms after exposure.

17|14|Type II hypersensitivity|What distinguishes a typical type II reaction from type III?|Antibodies target antigens on cell surfaces rather than deposited soluble immune complexes|It is mediated only by delayed T cells|It involves no antibodies|It always requires inhaled pollen|Cell-bound antigens are the characteristic targets in cytotoxic type II hypersensitivity.

17|14,18|Type II mechanism|Which mechanism can cause hemolysis in an incompatible blood transfusion?|Antibody binding activates complement against donor erythrocytes|IgE makes every erythrocyte divide|T cells produce a new bacterial toxin|A fungal spore invades the blood bag|Antibodies recognizing incompatible red-cell antigens can trigger agglutination and complement-mediated damage.

17|15,16,17|ABO groups|Which antibodies are expected in a person with type A blood in the simplified ABO scheme?|Anti-B|Anti-A only|Both anti-A and anti-B|Neither anti-A nor anti-B|Type A red cells carry A antigen, so anti-B rather than anti-A is expected in the usual ABO pattern.

17|15,16,17|ABO groups|Which ABO antigens are on type AB red blood cells?|Both A and B|Neither A nor B|A only|B only|The AB group expresses both antigen types and ordinarily lacks anti-A and anti-B antibodies.

17|15,16,17|ABO groups|Ignoring Rh and other compatibility factors, which packed red cells can a type O recipient receive?|Type O only|Type AB only|Types A and B only|Any ABO group|Type O recipients normally have anti-A and anti-B, so A- or B-bearing donor red cells are incompatible in the simplified model.

17|15,16,17|ABO groups|Why can type O packed red cells be useful in the simplified ABO donor model?|Their red cells lack A and B antigens|Their plasma always lacks every antibody|Their red cells express both A and B antigens|They contain no hemoglobin|The statement concerns donor red-cell antigens; real transfusion compatibility includes additional factors and testing.

17|18|Transfusion reactions|Why can an ABO-incompatible transfusion damage kidneys?|Hemolysis and systemic effects can follow antibody-mediated red-cell injury|Donor red cells automatically become bacteria|IgA directly blocks all kidney tubules in every transfusion|All red cells normally contain bacterial endotoxin|The lecture lists kidney failure among possible consequences of severe transfusion reactions.

17|19|Hemolytic disease|Which maternal-fetal Rh combination can create risk of Rh-related hemolytic disease after sensitization?|Rh-negative mother and Rh-positive fetus|Rh-positive mother and Rh-negative fetus only|Both mother and fetus lacking Rh antigen|Only two Rh-negative parents with an Rh-negative fetus|Maternal sensitization to fetal Rh antigens can lead to antibodies against Rh-positive fetal red cells.

17|19,20,21|Placental antibodies|Which antibody class can cross the placenta and contribute to Rh-related hemolytic disease?|IgG|IgM pentamer|IgD only|Secretory IgA dimer|IgG crosses the placenta; large IgM does not cross in the same way.

17|20,21|Rh prevention|What is the immunologic purpose of anti-D immune globulin in the lecture's prevention example?|Reduce maternal sensitization to fetal Rh-positive red cells|Stimulate the mother to make more anti-D memory cells|Convert the fetus from Rh-positive to Rh-negative|Destroy every maternal B cell|Passive anti-D targets fetal Rh-positive red cells entering maternal circulation before an active sensitization response develops.

17|23,25|Type III hypersensitivity|What initiates tissue injury in immune-complex hypersensitivity?|Persistence and deposition of antigen-antibody complexes|Only direct IgE binding to pollen|Only lack of thymic development|A bacterial endospore becoming a macrophage|Deposited immune complexes can activate complement and recruit damaging inflammation.

17|24,26|Type III examples|How does an Arthus reaction differ from serum sickness in the examples given?|Arthus is localized; serum sickness is systemic|Arthus is type IV; serum sickness is type I|Arthus never involves antibodies|Serum sickness always targets only donor red cells|Both are immune-complex examples, but their distribution and clinical setting differ.

17|27|Type IV hypersensitivity|Which mediators are central to delayed type IV hypersensitivity?|Sensitized T cells and recruited macrophages|Only IgE on mast cells|Only anti-A IgM on erythrocytes|Only soluble IgG complexes in joints|Type IV is cell-mediated; cytokine release from sensitized T cells promotes the delayed response.

17|28|Tuberculin response|What produces the indurated area in the tuberculin test example?|A delayed cellular response involving sensitized T cells|Immediate IgE-mediated airway closure|Direct lysis of donor red cells by anti-B|Instant conversion of all skin cells into plasma cells|The lecture uses the skin test as an example of delayed hypersensitivity rather than immediate allergy.

17|29|Contact dermatitis|An itchy skin reaction develops after poison-ivy exposure through a delayed T-cell response. Which category fits?|Type IV|Type I only|Type II|Type III|The lecture classifies allergic contact dermatitis as a cell-mediated delayed reaction.

17|5,30|Hypersensitivity comparison|Which complete pairing is correct?|I: IgE; II: cell-targeting antibodies; III: immune complexes; IV: T cells|I: T cells; II: IgE; III: red cells only; IV: IgM|All four are exclusively IgE-mediated|All four are forms of immunodeficiency|The four categories are distinguished by their dominant immune mechanism and target context.

15|3,4|Innate immunity|Which defense is present without prior exposure to a particular antigen?|Innate immunity|An antigen-specific secondary antibody response|Vaccine-induced memory only|Clonal expansion of one antigen-specific B cell|Innate defenses provide preexisting barriers and responses; adaptive responses are antigen-specific and can develop memory.

15|5|Recognition|What is an antigen in the immune-recognition context of the lecture?|A substance recognized by the immune system as a target|Only a whole living bacterium|Only a red blood cell|Any drug that lowers a fever|Antigens can be cell-surface molecules, foreign particles or other molecular structures, not just entire microbes.

15|6,7,8,9|Lymphatic system|Which is a normal function of the lymphatic system?|Return excess tissue fluid to the circulation|Pump oxygen directly into erythrocytes|Produce bile in the gallbladder|Carry only arterial blood from the heart|The lymphatic system drains excess fluid, transports absorbed fats and supports immune defenses.

15|7|Lymph flow|Where are foreign agents filtered from lymph by concentrated immune cells?|Lymph nodes|Only cardiac valves|Only lung alveoli|The renal pelvis|Lymph passes through lymph nodes before returning to the bloodstream.

15|10|Lymphatic organs|Where do T cells undergo their major maturation process?|Thymus|Spleen only|Adult gallbladder|Blood plasma|T cells originate from marrow-derived precursors and develop in the thymus.

15|10|Lymphatic organs|Where do B cells differentiate in adults?|Bone marrow|Thymic cortex only|Skin keratin|The lens of the eye|The course contrasts adult B-cell development in bone marrow with T-cell development in the thymus.

15|11|Lymphatic organs|Which lymphatic organ filters blood rather than lymph?|Spleen|A lymph node|A lymphatic capillary|A tonsillar crypt alone|The spleen contains phagocytes and lymphocytes positioned to monitor blood.

15|11|Mucosal defenses|What are Peyer's patches?|Lymphoid nodules associated with the small intestine|Enzymes that digest bacterial walls|Antibodies bound to mast cells|Blood-clotting proteins|Peyer's patches are part of gut-associated lymphoid tissue and contain immune cells.

15|11|Mucosal defenses|What is the role of intestinal M cells described in the slide notes?|Transfer sampled material to underlying lymphoid tissue|Make red blood cells from iron|Secrete every class of antibody|Remove all intestinal nutrients|Microfold cells transport material across the epithelium to support mucosal immune surveillance.

15|12|Phagocyte network|What does the mononuclear phagocyte system emphasize?|A distributed network of tissue phagocytes|Only antibodies dissolved in plasma|Only keratinized skin cells|Only bacterial endospores|The lecture describes a phagocyte-containing tissue network extending across organs.

15|14,15,18|Skin barrier|How does intact skin help prevent infection?|Tightly packed epithelial cells and keratin limit entry|It produces a different antibody for every organism immediately|It lacks all resident microbiota|It permits unrestricted passage of bacteria|Skin provides a physical barrier and chemical defenses; breaks in it create entry opportunities.

15|16,18|Mucosal defenses|How do airway mucus and cilia help protect against microbes?|Trap material and move it toward removal|Generate antigen-specific memory B cells directly|Convert all viruses into bacteria|Replace every macrophage|Mucus traps particles while ciliary movement helps clear them from respiratory surfaces.

15|17|Chemical barriers|Which antimicrobial substance degrades bacterial peptidoglycan?|Lysozyme|Histamine|IgE|Perforin|Lysozyme in secretions such as tears and saliva targets bacterial cell-wall material.

15|17|Chemical barriers|How do lactoferrin and transferrin limit microbial growth?|They bind iron and reduce its availability to microbes|They add iron directly to every bacterial cell|They digest only viral capsids|They act as bacterial flagella|Iron sequestration is a chemical defense because many microbes require iron for enzyme function.

15|17,47|Antimicrobial peptides|What is a major direct action of defensins?|Disrupting microbial membranes by forming pores|Producing bacterial capsules|Converting nitrate into nitrite|Changing antibody class|Defensins are antimicrobial peptides that can damage membrane integrity.

15|19,20|Hematopoiesis|What does hematopoiesis mean?|Production of blood cells|Production of microbial endotoxin|Breakdown of antibodies by bacteria|Migration of a virus into a nucleus|Blood cells arise from stem-cell lineages, with differentiation directing the eventual cell type.

15|21,22,23|Neutrophils|Which cells are rapid phagocytic responders at a site of infection?|Neutrophils|Erythrocytes|Plasma cells|Platelets only|The lecture places neutrophils among the earliest phagocytes arriving at infected tissue.

15|23|Eosinophils|Which task is especially associated with eosinophils?|Defense against parasitic worms|Secretion of all circulating IgG|Production of the skin's keratin|Direct synthesis of bacterial peptidoglycan|Eosinophils release toxic granule products, including major basic protein, that can damage large parasites.

15|24|Histamine|Which pair of cells contains histamine-rich granules involved in allergy and inflammation?|Basophils and mast cells|Erythrocytes and platelets|Plasma cells and memory B cells|Only cytotoxic T cells|Basophils circulate and mast cells reside in tissues; both can release histamine.

15|24,26|Macrophage development|What does a circulating monocyte commonly become after entering tissue?|A macrophage|A red blood cell|A fungal hypha|An antibody molecule|Monocytes can differentiate into larger tissue phagocytes with abundant lysosomal machinery.

15|25|Antigen-presenting cells|Why are dendritic cells important to the transition toward adaptive immunity?|They present antigen to T cells|They are the main source of erythrocytes|They convert antibodies into antigens|They replace the thymus|Dendritic cells take up material and present processed antigen, linking detection to lymphocyte activation.
15|27|Tissue phagocytes|Which tissue contains Kupffer cells?|Liver|Brain|Lung alveoli|Bone cortex|The lecture associates Kupffer cells with liver and microglia with brain tissue.

15|27|Tissue phagocytes|Which immune cells are associated with the brain in the lecture's tissue-phagocyte list?|Microglia|Kupffer cells|Alveolar macrophages|Plasma erythrocytes|Microglia are resident immune cells of the central nervous system.

15|29,30|Phagocytosis|What does chemotaxis describe?|Directed movement toward a chemical signal|Antibody class switching|Random rupture of red blood cells|Production of a bacterial endospore|Chemical signals from damaged tissue, microbes or immune cells guide phagocytes toward the affected site.

15|31|Pattern recognition|Which pairing correctly relates a receptor to its target category?|Pattern-recognition receptor and a microbial PAMP|IgE and an erythrocyte nucleus in every allergy|Catalase and an MHC peptide|A T-cell receptor and mannitol fermentation|Innate receptors detect shared microbial patterns rather than requiring a unique antibody to every organism.

15|31|Pattern recognition|Which molecule is a PAMP associated with Gram-negative bacteria?|Lipopolysaccharide|Human serum albumin|Host keratin|A thyroid hormone|LPS can be recognized by innate pattern-recognition pathways, including the TLR4 pathway discussed in the lecture.

15|32|Opsonization|Why can antibody or complement coating enhance phagocytosis?|Phagocytes can more readily bind the coated target|It always prevents all phagocyte adhesion|It converts a pathogen into a host cell|It removes every antigen from the microbe|Opsonization marks a target for recognition and uptake by phagocytic cells.

15|32,33|Phagocytosis|What forms when a phagosome fuses with a lysosome?|Phagolysosome|Plasma cell|Bacterial capsule|Antibody pentamer|Fusion brings the engulfed material together with degradative enzymes and antimicrobial components.

15|33|Phagocyte killing|Which products can contribute to oxygen-dependent killing inside phagocytes?|Reactive oxygen and nitrogen compounds|Only secreted lactose|Only fungal chitin|Only the Fc region of IgD|The lecture lists peroxide, superoxide, nitric oxide and hypochlorite among toxic products used against engulfed pathogens.

15|34,35,36|Inflammation|Which set contains the four classic signs of inflammation described in the course?|Redness, warmth, swelling and pain|Cough, jaundice, blindness and paralysis|Only antibody production and memory|Only fever and low blood sugar|Increased blood flow, fluid movement and inflammatory mediators contribute to these local findings.

15|35|Inflammation|How does histamine help produce redness and warmth at an injured site?|It promotes vasodilation and increased local blood flow|It prevents any blood from reaching the area|It destroys all lymphocytes|It converts plasma directly into bacteria|Vasodilation increases perfusion; increased vascular permeability also contributes to fluid accumulation.

15|35,37|Diapedesis|What happens during leukocyte diapedesis?|Cells move through vessel walls into tissue|Antibodies change from IgM to IgG|A bacterium divides by budding|Lymph returns through the thoracic duct only|Diapedesis is passage of leukocytes across the vascular endothelium.

15|35|Inflammation|What contributes to pus at an infected site?|Dead phagocytes, tissue debris and microbial remnants|Only viable red blood cells|Only newly synthesized antibodies|Only unused vaccine ingredients|Pus reflects accumulated products of the inflammatory response, including dead immune cells and debris.

15|38|Fever|Where do pyrogen-driven signals act to raise the temperature set point?|Hypothalamus|Bone marrow only|Spleen only|Small-intestinal lumen|Fever involves a regulated increase in the hypothalamic temperature set point.

15|38|Fever mediators|Which pair is listed as endogenous pyrogenic cytokines?|IL-1 and TNF|IgA and IgD|Catalase and oxidase|Chitin and cellulose|Immune-cell cytokines stimulate pathways involving prostaglandins that contribute to fever.

15|39|Fever|Which effect can help explain a defensive benefit of a moderate fever?|Conditions become less favorable for some pathogens and immune reactions accelerate|Every fever guarantees immediate sterilization|Fever eliminates the need for all immune cells|All microbial enzymes work best at higher temperatures|The lecture describes several potential benefits while recognizing that excessive temperature can be harmful.

15|40,41,42,43|Interferon|How do type I interferon signals help neighboring cells resist viral infection?|They induce antiviral proteins that interfere with replication|They directly become viral capsids|They make bacterial peptidoglycan|They convert every uninfected cell into a plasma cell|Signals from virus-infected cells induce antiviral defenses in nearby cells.

15|42|Interferon|Which effect is associated with interferon-gamma in the lecture?|Activation of macrophages and other immune cells|Formation of bacterial endospores|Lactose fermentation|Direct red-cell agglutination by IgM|Interferon-gamma functions as an immune-activating cytokine rather than an antibody.

15|44,45|Complement|Which complement pathway is initiated by antigen-bound antibodies?|Classical pathway|Alternative pathway only|Lectin pathway only|Glycolysis|Classical complement activation links antigen-antibody binding to downstream complement effects.

15|44,45|Complement|What is a major outcome of membrane attack complex formation?|Pore formation that can lyse susceptible microbes|Production of a new antibody isotype|Differentiation of a red blood cell|Increased fungal budding only|Complement terminal components assemble a membrane-disrupting complex on susceptible targets.
